Convergent boundary, middle stage. The plates move towards each other. A mountain range stands along the boundary. On the front face the rock layers bend up under the range, and the crust beneath it is thicker: a deep root, reaching much deeper than the range stands high. The front face stands at the front of the block.

captures.note: Divergent, late stage: rift, inked scarps with ticks, lakes.
captures.text: Divergent boundary, late stage. The plates move apart. A deep rift valley lies along the boundary between stepped fault scarps, with slightly raised shoulders on either side and lakes on its floor. On the front face the rock layers drop at each fault, and the crust beneath the rift is thinner. The front face stands at the front of the block.

Transform boundary, late stage. The plates slide past each other. The ridges and stream valleys that cross the boundary are clearly offset sideways along a straight fault: looking across the boundary, the far side has moved to the right. The land is not raised or lowered, and on the front face the rock layers and the crust are unchanged. The front face stands at the front of the block.

A deep rift valley lies along the boundary between stepped fault scarps, with slightly raised shoulders on either side and lakes on its floor. On the front face the rock layers drop at each fault, and the crust beneath the rift is thinner. The front face stands at the front of the block. The dotted line on the front face is the convergent profile at the same stage: there the land stands high in a range over a deep root. The dash-dot line on the front face is the transform profile at the same stage: there the land keeps the starting height and crust.
